paragraphs: Let us take it as an established truth, then, that in case of disunion the individual States, or such combinations of them as might be formed out of the wreck of the general Confederacy, would be subject to those swings between peace and war, friendship and enmity, which have been the lot of all neighboring nations not united under one government. On that assumption, let us look briefly at some of the consequences that such a situation would bring.

War between the States, in the first period of their separate existence, would bring far greater suffering than it commonly does in those countries where regular military establishments have long been in place. The disciplined armies always kept on foot in continental Europe have a threatening aspect toward liberty and economy. Nevertheless they have had one signal advantage: they have made sudden conquests impracticable and have prevented the rapid devastation that used to mark the progress of war before they were introduced. The art of fortification has served the same ends. The nations of Europe are ringed with chains of fortified places, which obstruct invasion at every point. Whole campaigns are wasted in reducing two or three frontier garrisons in order to gain entry into an enemy's country. Similar obstacles meet an invader at every step, exhausting his strength and slowing his progress. Formerly an invading army would penetrate into the heart of a neighboring country almost as soon as word of its approach could arrive. Now a comparatively small force of disciplined troops, acting on the defensive and aided by fortified posts, can impede and finally defeat the enterprises of a much larger one. The history of war in that part of the world is no longer a history of nations subdued and empires overturned. It is a history of towns taken and retaken; of battles that decide nothing; of retreats more beneficial than victories; of much effort and little gain.

In this country the scene would be entirely reversed. Jealousy of military establishments would put them off as long as possible. The lack of fortifications, leaving the frontiers of one State open to another, would make invasions easy. The populous States would overrun their less populous neighbors with little difficulty. Conquests would be as easy to make as they would be hard to hold. War, therefore, would be irregular and predatory. PLUNDER and devastation always march in the train of irregular troops. The sufferings of individuals would make the principal figure in the events that characterized our military exploits.

This picture is not too highly colored, though I admit it would not long remain accurate. Safety from external danger is the most powerful director of national conduct. Even the ardent love of liberty will, after a time, give way to its dictates. The violent destruction of life and property that comes with war, and the continual effort and alarm of a state of continual danger, will compel even the nations most attached to liberty to seek repose and security in institutions that tend to destroy their civil and political rights. To be safer, they at length become willing to run the risk of being less free.

The institutions I chiefly have in mind are STANDING ARMIES and the accompanying apparatus of military establishments. It is said that standing armies are not provided against in the new Constitution, and it is therefore inferred that they may exist under it.(1) By the very terms of that argument, however, their existence is at most doubtful and uncertain. But standing armies, it may be answered, must inevitably result from a dissolution of the Confederacy. Frequent war and constant apprehension, which require a state of equally constant preparation, will infallibly produce them. The weaker States or confederacies would turn to them first, to put themselves on an equality with their more powerful neighbors. They would try to make up for inferior population and resources with a more regular and effective system of defense: disciplined troops and fortifications. At the same time they would be forced to strengthen the executive arm of government, and in doing so their constitutions would move progressively toward monarchy. It is in the nature of war to increase the executive at the expense of the legislative authority.

The expedients just mentioned would soon give the States or confederacies that used them a superiority over their neighbors. Small states, or states of less natural strength, under vigorous governments and with the help of disciplined armies, have often triumphed over large states, or states of greater natural strength, that lacked these advantages. Neither the pride nor the safety of the more important States or confederacies would let them submit for long to this mortifying and artificial superiority. They would quickly turn to means like those by which it had been achieved, in order to regain their lost pre-eminence. Thus we should see established in every part of this country, in a short time, the same engines of despotism that have been the scourge of the Old World. This, at least, would be the natural course of things, and our reasonings will be the more likely to be sound in proportion as they conform to that standard.

These conclusions are not vague inferences from supposed or speculative defects in a Constitution that places all power in the hands of the people or of their representatives and delegates. They are sound conclusions, drawn from the natural and necessary course of human affairs.

It may perhaps be asked, as an objection to this, why standing armies did not spring up out of the contentions that so often distracted the ancient republics of Greece. Different answers, equally satisfactory, may be given to this question. The industrious habits of the people of the present day, absorbed in the pursuit of gain and devoted to the improvement of agriculture and commerce, are incompatible with the condition of a nation of soldiers, which was the true condition of the people of those republics. The means of revenue have been greatly multiplied by the increase of gold and silver and of the industrial arts. The science of finance, which is the offspring of modern times, has joined with the habits of nations to produce an entire revolution in the system of war. Together they have made disciplined armies, distinct from the body of the citizens, the inseparable companions of frequent hostility.

There is also a wide difference between military establishments in a country that its situation seldom exposes to invasion within its borders and those in a country that is often subject to such invasions and always fears them. The rulers of the former can have no good pretext, even if they are so inclined, for keeping on foot armies as numerous as must necessarily be maintained in the latter. In the first case these armies are rarely, if ever, called into action for internal defense, so the people are in no danger of being broken to military subordination. The laws are not accustomed to relaxations in favor of military necessities. The civil state remains in full vigor, neither corrupted nor confused with the principles or tendencies of the other state. The smallness of the army makes the natural strength of the community more than a match for it. The citizens, not accustomed to look to the military power for protection or to submit to its oppressions, neither love nor fear the soldiery. They regard them with a spirit of jealous acquiescence in a necessary evil, and stand ready to resist a power that they suppose may be used to the prejudice of their rights.

Under such circumstances the army may usefully aid the public official in suppressing a small faction, or an occasional mob or insurrection. But it will be unable to enforce encroachments against the united efforts of the great body of the people.

In a country in the situation last described, the opposite of all this happens. The perpetual threat of danger obliges the government to be always prepared to repel it, and its armies must be numerous enough for instant defense. The continual need for their services raises the importance of the soldier and lowers the condition of the citizen in proportion. The military state becomes elevated above the civil. The inhabitants of territories that are often the theater of war are unavoidably subjected to frequent infringements of their rights, which weaken their sense of those rights. By degrees the people come to regard the soldiery not only as their protectors but as their superiors. The step from this disposition to regarding them as masters is neither distant nor difficult. But it is very difficult to bring a people under such impressions to make a bold or effective resistance to usurpations backed by military power.

The kingdom of Great Britain falls within the first description. Its situation as an island, and a powerful navy, guard it in great measure against the possibility of foreign invasion and remove the need for a numerous army within the kingdom. A force sufficient to hold out against a sudden landing until the militia could have time to rally and assemble is all that has been thought necessary. No motive of national policy has demanded, nor would public opinion have tolerated, a larger number of troops on its domestic establishment. For a long time there has been little room for the operation of the other causes that I have listed as consequences of internal war. This peculiarly fortunate situation has contributed in great degree to preserve the liberty that the country enjoys to this day, in spite of its prevalent venality and corruption. If, on the contrary, Britain had been situated on the continent and had been compelled by that situation, as she would have been, to make her military establishments at home as large as those of the other great powers of Europe, she would in all probability, like them, be a victim today to the absolute power of a single man. It is possible, though not easy, that the people of that island may be enslaved from other causes. But it cannot be by the prowess of an army as small as the one usually kept up within the kingdom.

If we are wise enough to preserve the Union, we may for ages enjoy an advantage similar to that of an island situation. Europe is at a great distance from us. Her colonies in our vicinity will probably continue to be too far out of proportion to us in strength to be able to give us any dangerous annoyance. Extensive military establishments cannot, in this position, be necessary to our security. But if we should be disunited, and the separate parts should either remain apart or, which is most probable, be thrown together into two or three confederacies, we should in a short time be in the situation of the continental powers of Europe. Our liberties would fall prey to the means of defending ourselves against one another's ambition and jealousy.

This idea is not superficial or trivial but solid and weighty. It deserves the most serious and mature consideration of every prudent and honest man, of whatever party. Let such men stop firmly and solemnly, and reflect without passion on how important this idea is. Let them view it from every side and follow it to all its consequences. Then they will not hesitate to give up trivial objections to a Constitution whose rejection would in all probability put a final end to the Union. The airy phantoms that flit before the disordered imaginations of some of its adversaries would quickly give way to the more substantial shapes of dangers that are real, certain and formidable.
